m8-t1.introduction: A second way to understand “Resume & portfolio building with AI”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Make the résumé readable to people and parsers
sections.explanation: Clear text, meaningful headings and truthful role vocabulary help readers locate relevant evidence. Parser behaviour varies.

items.label: Read the role
items.detail: Identify the tasks and evidence the employer requests.

items.label: Choose relevant facts
items.detail: Use skills and experience you can substantiate.

items.label: Use a clear structure
items.detail: Keep text and section headings easy to extract and read.

items.label: Inspect the export
items.detail: Check parsing, links and the actual final document.

sections.takeaway: Test the submitted file and follow the employer’s requested format rather than claiming a universal ATS guarantee.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: An achievement is a claim with a source
sections.explanation: Action, task, result and evidence make a contribution concrete. Numbers should come from records rather than invented impact.

items.label: Action
items.detail: Name what you actually did.

items.label: Task
items.detail: Describe the specific work and context.

items.label: Result
items.detail: State only the outcome the evidence supports.

items.label: Evidence
items.detail: Link a safe artefact or record that substantiates the claim.

sections.takeaway: A measured classroom output must not be presented as paid work or an unobserved business result.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Tailor by selecting and editing, not inventing
sections.explanation: AI can help compare a job description with existing evidence. It cannot create a missing qualification or experience.

items.label: Extract requirements
items.detail: Read the actual job description’s priorities.

items.label: Map evidence
items.detail: Match your genuine projects and skills to those needs.

items.label: Edit truthfully
items.detail: Reorder or tighten wording without adding unsupported claims.

items.label: Verify the final
items.detail: Check every number, title, date and contribution.

sections.takeaway: Leave an unsupported requirement as a gap and decide honestly whether or how to apply.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 3. Tailoring with AI as an editor

sections.title: A portfolio connects the story to inspectable work
sections.explanation: A case study should make the problem, contribution, outcome and limitations easy to verify.

items.label: Problem
items.detail: State the user need or practice question.

items.label: Contribution
items.detail: Distinguish your decisions and work from the team’s.

items.label: Artefact
items.detail: Link the permitted document, demo or analysis.

items.label: Learning and limits
items.detail: Explain corrections, unknowns and what you would change.

sections.takeaway: Publish only a safe version of evidence and credit team work and AI assistance accurately.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Integrity survives the editing tool
sections.explanation: Application claims belong to you regardless of who helped polish the wording. Employer policies can differ.

items.label: Check the rule
items.detail: Read the specific application’s instructions.

items.label: Use your facts
items.detail: Keep content tied to your own evidence.

items.label: Review every claim
items.detail: Remove invented achievements or exaggerated results.

items.label: Answer honestly
items.detail: Explain assistance and your responsibility for the submission.

sections.takeaway: Disclose assistance when requested or required, and never upload other people’s confidential information to prepare an application.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. AI-use in applications: disclosure and integrity

checkpoint.question: If an assistant adds a plausible percentage improvement to a résumé bullet, can you keep it?
checkpoint.answer: Only if your own evidence supports it. Otherwise remove it; a persuasive number is not a measured result.

m8-t2.introduction: A second way to understand “LinkedIn & your professional brand”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Be findable, credible and specific
sections.explanation: A professional profile should help the right reader connect a truthful skill claim to evidence of work.

items.label: Findable
items.detail: Use genuine role and skill terms relevant to your goal.

items.label: Credible
items.detail: Link real artefacts and consistent evidence.

items.label: Specific
items.detail: Describe actual tasks and contribution instead of vague superlatives.

items.label: Appropriate
items.detail: Respect privacy, rights and employer or institution rules.

sections.takeaway: Visibility is useful only when the claims remain accurate and appropriate to share.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. What LinkedIn is for (and what it is not)

sections.title: Each profile section has a communication job
sections.explanation: Identity, headline, summary and evidence should tell the same truthful story without implying qualifications you do not hold.

items.label: Identity
items.detail: Use an accurate name and an appropriate image.

items.label: Headline and summary
items.detail: State your current focus and supported strengths.

items.label: Experience and projects
items.detail: Describe actual responsibilities and label simulations.

items.label: Featured evidence
items.detail: Offer safe links to relevant work and current contact routes.

sections.takeaway: A classroom project title is not an executive appointment or an external credential.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Share a concrete learning story
sections.explanation: A useful post can explain an artefact, a correction or an evidence-based lesson instead of generating empty professional slogans.

items.label: Choose real work
items.detail: Pick a project or learning event you can substantiate.

items.label: Explain a decision
items.detail: Name the problem and what you actually changed.

items.label: Show safe evidence
items.detail: Use permitted excerpts and truthful context.

items.label: Listen and improve
items.detail: Respond to questions and correct mistakes openly.

sections.takeaway: Do not publish another person’s image, quotation or confidential work without appropriate permission.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Outreach should respect the recipient’s time
sections.explanation: A specific, truthful question gives someone a manageable way to help. It does not create an obligation to reply.

items.label: Find relevance
items.detail: Identify a genuine shared context or role interest.

items.label: Write a short note
items.detail: Introduce yourself truthfully and ask a specific question.

items.label: Offer context
items.detail: Link relevant safe evidence only when useful.

items.label: Follow up respectfully
items.detail: Keep boundaries and record learning without pressuring the person.

sections.takeaway: Avoid bulk pretending-to-be-personal messages and respect a refusal or silence.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: A professional brand is a consistency check
sections.explanation: The same result should mean the same thing across a résumé, profile and portfolio. Consistency cannot rescue an invented claim.

items.label: Compare the versions
items.detail: Check dates, titles, figures and your role.

items.label: Review permissions
items.detail: Remove private or unapproved material.

items.label: Credit fairly
items.detail: Distinguish personal, team and AI-assisted work.

items.label: Correct the record
items.detail: Update misleading or stale statements rather than repeating them.

sections.takeaway: Keep identity, contribution, privacy and disclosure accurate in every public version.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Can you call yourself the CEO of a classroom prototype to make a profile sound stronger?
checkpoint.answer: Do not imply a real appointment or business experience you do not have. Describe the course project and your actual contribution honestly.

m8-t3.introduction: A second way to understand “Professional writing & email with AI”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: Put the reader’s next action first
sections.explanation: A workplace message should make its purpose and required action easy to find before adding background.

items.label: Bottom line
items.detail: State the decision, status or request clearly.

items.label: Relevant context
items.detail: Include only what the reader needs to understand it.

items.label: Required action
items.detail: Name the owner, requested response and real deadline.

items.label: Check the close
items.detail: Confirm the next step and contact route.

sections.takeaway: Do not make a commitment or state an approval beyond your authority.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 1. Writing for the reader's next action

sections.title: Different emails need different opening information
sections.explanation: The message pattern should fit what the reader must do, rather than a generic formal introduction.

items.label: Request
items.detail: Name what you need and the relevant response time.

items.label: Update
items.detail: State the current status and what changed.

items.label: Follow-up
items.detail: Refer to the earlier request and make the next action clear.

items.label: Bad news
items.detail: State the fact, limits and recovery plan without invented blame.

sections.takeaway: Use verified dates and facts; do not let a template invent details.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. Email patterns you will use weekly

sections.title: Documents should separate evidence from decisions
sections.explanation: Reports, proposals and minutes have different jobs and must retain the right source trail.

items.label: Report
items.detail: Connect the question, findings, limitations and recommendation.

items.label: Proposal
items.detail: Describe a change, risks, test and requested authority.

items.label: Minutes
items.detail: Record actual decisions, actions, owners and unresolved points.

sections.takeaway: A generated meeting summary cannot create an agreement that participants never made.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Use the assistant as an editor with boundaries
sections.explanation: Provide verified facts and a clear reader, then inspect whether the edit altered meaning or introduced promises.

items.label: Supply a factual brief
items.detail: Name the audience, purpose and authorised facts.

items.label: Request a bounded draft
items.detail: Specify style, length and prohibited inventions.

items.label: Compare meaning
items.detail: Check every added or changed claim against the brief.

items.label: Approve your version
items.detail: Make the final wording your responsibility.

sections.takeaway: Keep sensitive material out of unapproved tools and retain your own judgement on consequential wording.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 4. AI as a writing partner — the discipline

sections.title: A pre-send check is a final action gate
sections.explanation: Correct content can still harm when it reaches the wrong recipient or carries an unintended attachment.

items.label: Verify facts
items.detail: Check names, amounts, dates and links.

items.label: Verify authority
items.detail: Confirm commitments and approvals are real.

items.label: Verify recipients
items.detail: Check addresses, reply-all, sharing and attachments.

items.label: Read for meaning
items.detail: Inspect tone, next action and required disclosure.

sections.takeaway: Review recipients, authority, sensitive content and the actual attachments—not only grammar.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: You remain accountable for the signed message
sections.explanation: A personal style file can make assistance more consistent, but it does not transfer authorship or responsibility to the tool.

items.label: Keep useful patterns
items.detail: Record appropriate openings, structures and voice examples.

items.label: Adapt to the reader
items.detail: Choose a register that fits the actual relationship.

items.label: Own the final
items.detail: Approve only claims and commitments you can defend.

items.label: Learn from corrections
items.detail: Update the template when a repeated problem appears.

sections.takeaway: If a message is wrong, correct it and improve the checking workflow.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: If AI drafted the email, who is responsible for an invented deadline in the sent message?
checkpoint.answer: The sender remains responsible. Verify dates, commitments, recipients and attachments before sending and correct an error promptly.

m8-t4.introduction: A second way to understand “Interview & communication practice; the AI-era job map”: read the original explanation, follow the diagram and play or step through its focus points. All practice stays separate from your reading and quiz requirements.

sections.title: A STAR story needs your action and evidence
sections.explanation: Use a real course, work or volunteer example and explain your personal responsibility. A simulation should stay labelled as one.

items.label: Situation
items.detail: Give enough real context to understand the problem.

items.label: Task
items.detail: State what you were responsible for.

items.label: Action
items.detail: Describe your actual decisions and contribution.

items.label: Result and learning
items.detail: Show supported outcomes and what you changed or learned.

sections.takeaway: Do not invent experience to fill a story structure.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Explain your AI use with a concrete boundary
sections.explanation: An employer learns more from a specific checked workflow than a list of tools or a claim to use AI for everything.

items.label: Where it helps
items.detail: Name a task and the assistance you actually used.

items.label: How you check
items.detail: Explain evidence, calculations or review that kept it honest.

items.label: Where you stop
items.detail: Describe privacy, authority and judgement boundaries.

items.label: What you built
items.detail: Show a safe artefact and your contribution.

sections.takeaway: Include a real correction or refusal to delegate work you could not safely verify.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 2. The "how do you use AI" answer

sections.title: A mock interview is rehearsal, not a hiring verdict
sections.explanation: Practice can improve clarity and evidence, but a model’s feedback is not an employer’s validated assessment.

items.label: Use the real role
items.detail: Provide an appropriate public job description.

items.label: Answer one question
items.detail: Practise with your own evidence and voice.

items.label: Review feedback
items.detail: Check relevance and challenge unsupported scoring.

items.label: Revise and test
items.detail: Try again and include human feedback where possible.

sections.takeaway: Do not let rehearsal rewrite your history or claim a predicted hiring outcome.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Communication practice includes listening and permission
sections.explanation: A presentation or discussion needs clear contributions, respectful response and appropriate handling of recordings.

items.label: Frame the issue
items.detail: Define scope and the question before arguing.

items.label: Add evidence
items.detail: Make one supported point and connect to others.

items.label: Listen and respond
items.detail: Build on or challenge an idea with reasons.

items.label: Review safely
items.detail: Record only with permission and use feedback constructively.

sections.takeaway: Do not equate speaking volume or a model’s score with contribution quality.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

sections.title: Search by tasks and evidence, not a fashionable title
sections.explanation: Roles vary across employers. Match the job description’s tasks to the work you can demonstrate.

items.label: Commerce tasks
items.detail: Show checked calculations, reports or reconciliation workflows.

items.label: Management tasks
items.detail: Show process, project and communication evidence.

items.label: Arts and communication
items.detail: Show verified research, writing or multilingual content.

items.label: Science tasks
items.detail: Show reproducible methods, units and evidence review.

sections.takeaway: Course completion does not guarantee a job, regulated authority or an external professional credential.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.
sections.section: 5. The AI-era job map for non-technical graduates

sections.title: A career plan is a reviewable learning loop
sections.explanation: Preparation, applications and interview learning should inform the next block of work rather than produce an activity count alone.

items.label: Prepare evidence
items.detail: Finish a truthful résumé, portfolio and relevant practice.

items.label: Apply deliberately
items.detail: Choose roles and outreach that fit your actual capabilities.

items.label: Track feedback
items.detail: Record responses, gaps and interview learning.

items.label: Revise the plan
items.detail: Improve one skill or artefact and review the next step.

sections.takeaway: Use honest targeted applications and revise from evidence; no plan guarantees an offer.
sections.caption: Illustrative teaching model, not live results, a tool screenshot or an additional assessment requirement.

checkpoint.question: Does a mock interview score predict whether an employer will hire you?
checkpoint.answer: No. It is practice feedback. Use it critically, keep your examples truthful and seek human review rather than treating a model score as a hiring verdict.
